html:
Mansa Musa's pilgrimage was the hajj that Mansa Musa, king of the Mali Empire, made to Mecca in 1324 and 1325, crossing the Sahara and stopping in Cairo.

Arab writers describe a caravan of thousands of people, with camels carrying gold. Their numbers differ and are probably exaggerated, but they agree on the spending. In Cairo, then the capital of the Mamluk Sultanate, Musa gave gold to officials and spent it in the markets so freely that its value fell. The historian al-Umari, writing about twelve years later, said the price had still not recovered. On the way home Musa ran short and borrowed from Cairo merchants.

The journey changed how the world saw West Africa:

  • It showed North Africa and the Mediterranean how much gold came through the trans-Saharan trade.
  • European mapmakers put Mali on their maps; the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows Musa holding a gold nugget.
  • Musa brought back scholars and an architect, which helped make Timbuktu a centre of Islamic learning.
sum: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage was the hajj that Mansa Musa, king of the Mali Empire, made to Mecca in 1324 and 1325, crossing the Sahara and stopping in Cairo.
